title: The impurity of greed
hookLine: the impurity of the mind is greed, of the tongue lying (Asa di Var, ang 472)

lines: SOOTAK: IMPURITY AFTER BIRTH OR DEATH.
cards: Clean and dirty go deeper than germs. Shoes off at the door. Hands washed before eating.
A kitchen counter nobody puts a bag on. Families and cultures draw those lines in different places, and they matter.
In Guru Nanak's world, there was a strong idea called sootak: a time of ritual impurity that fell on a household after a birth or a death.
For a set period, the family was considered unclean, and others might avoid their food. Guru Nanak took that word and asked where impurity really lives.

teach.h: SOOTAK: AN OLD IDEA OF IMPURITY.
teach.b: The saloks are on ang 472, a short run of them. The first starts with a practical puzzle. If you believe in sootak, it says, in paraphrase, then sootak is everywhere.
There are tiny creatures in cow dung and in firewood.
Not a single grain of food is without life. Water itself gives life to everything. So how can anyone keep sootak out?
It's already in the kitchen. Then the answer: Nanak, sootak isn't removed that way. Only spiritual wisdom washes it off.
The next salok moves the word somewhere new. In paraphrase again: the sootak of the mind is greed. The sootak of the tongue is lying.
Tomorrow, the eyes and the ears. For today, stay with those two.
Lobh, greed, is the mind's impurity: the restless wanting that never says enough.

Koorh, the word from the salok of the false king, is the tongue's. A household can follow every rule after a birth and still have a greedy mind at the table. A person can scrub their hands and still lie with their mouth.
Guru Nanak isn't saying cleanliness doesn't matter; Sikh discipline includes bathing before the dawn prayers, and langar kitchens are kept clean.
He's saying the impurity that really keeps people from the One isn't on the skin. A third salok finishes the thought: all sootak is doubt, attachment to something second.
Birth and death come by the hukam, the divine order. They're not dirt. Greed and lying are.

how: Sikh practice keeps no period of ritual impurity after a birth or death; the Sikh Rehat Maryada sets such observances aside, and Sikhs hear these saloks in the dawn singing of Asa di Var.

games.q: where impurity lives — tap the pairs.
p: ritual impurity after birth or death

s: Guru Nanak says cleanliness doesn't matter
Sikh discipline includes bathing at dawn, and langar kitchens are kept clean; he says the impurity that matters most is inside.
the salok points out that every grain of food has life in it
so sootak, it says, is already in the kitchen.
the saloks call birth and death unclean
they say birth and death come by the hukam; greed and lying are the impurity.

games.q: a baby has just been born in a neighbor's house, and some say the home is unclean for a while. what do Guru Nanak's saloks say?
o: stay away until the period ends.
birth comes by the hukam; impurity is greed in the mind and lies on the tongue.
games.why: all sootak is doubt, the saloks say. birth and death come by the divine order. the real sootak is greed and lying.

practice: Rest your attention on your mouth for a moment, the tongue, the lips, the breath passing through.
Think of where a small untruth tends to slip out, an excuse, an exaggeration, a shaded story, and let the tongue rest, quiet and plain. If you pray, say Waheguru with that clean tongue.

wordCard.voice: Sootak. Ritual impurity, once thought to fall on a home after a birth or death. Guru Nanak moves it inside: the mind's sootak is greed, the tongue's is lying.
